subject: physical-sciences
title: States of Matter and the Particle Model

content.intro: All matter is made of particles. The arrangement, movement and spacing of these particles help explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.

sections.heading: Solids
sections.text: In a solid, particles are closely packed and vibrate around fixed positions. Solids usually have a definite shape and a definite volume.

sections.heading: Liquids
sections.text: In a liquid, particles remain close together but can move past one another. A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.

sections.heading: Gases
sections.text: In a gas, particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions. Gases do not have a fixed shape or volume and can be compressed.

content.example: When ice melts, its particles gain energy and move more freely. The substance changes from a solid to a liquid.
content.summary: The particle model explains matter through particle arrangement, movement and spacing. Heating can cause changes of state.

xh.title: Iimeko Zento NeModeli Yamasuntswana
xh.intro: Yonke into yenziwe ngamasuntswana. Indlela amasuntswana acwangciswe ngayo, ashukuma ngayo nashiyana ngayo inceda ukuchaza iimpawu zezinto eziqinileyo, ezilulwelo nezeegesi.
xh.summary: Imodeli yamasuntswana ichaza izinto ngokujonga indlela amasuntswana acwangciswe ngayo, ashukuma ngayo nashiyana ngayo.

quiz.question: How do particles in a solid generally behave?
options: They move freely and are far apart
They have no movement at all
They move only in straight lines
quiz.explanation: Particles in a solid vibrate around fixed positions, even though they do not move freely from place to place.

quiz.question: Which state of matter is generally easiest to compress?
quiz.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, so they can be pushed closer together.

quiz.question: What change of state occurs when a liquid becomes a gas?
quiz.explanation: Vaporisation is the change from a liquid to a gas.

content.intro: A force is an interaction that can change an object's motion or shape. Newton's laws describe how forces affect motion.

sections.heading: Newton's First Law
sections.text: An object remains at rest or continues moving at constant velocity in a straight line unless a non-zero resultant external force acts on it.

sections.heading: Newton's Second Law
sections.text: The resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration: Fnet = ma. Force is measured in newtons, mass in kilograms and acceleration in metres per second squared.

sections.heading: Newton's Third Law
sections.text: When object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on object A. These forces act on different objects.

content.example: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². Its resultant force is F = ma = 2 × 3 = 6 N.
content.summary: Newton's laws explain inertia, the relationship between resultant force and acceleration, and action-reaction force pairs.

xh.title: Amandla Nemithetho kaNewton
xh.intro: Amandla yintsebenziswano enokutshintsha intshukumo okanye imilo yento. Imithetho kaNewton ichaza indlela amandla ayichaphazela ngayo intshukumo.
xh.summary: Imithetho kaNewton ichaza inertia, unxulumano phakathi kwamandla nesantya sokutshintsha kwesantya, kunye nezibini zamandla alinganayo nachaseneyo.

quiz.question: Which equation represents Newton's Second Law?
quiz.explanation: Newton's Second Law states that resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.

quiz.question: What is the SI unit of force?
Action and reaction forces act on:
options: The same object in the same direction
Different objects in the same direction
quiz.explanation: Newton's Third Law force pairs are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and act on different objects.

content.intro: Electric circuits allow electric charge to flow through connected components. Voltage, current and resistance describe important aspects of circuit behaviour.

sections.heading: Electric current
sections.text: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge. It is measured in amperes (A). Current can be calculated using I = Q/t, where Q is charge in coulombs and t is time in seconds.

sections.heading: Potential difference and resistance
sections.text: Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge and is measured in volts (V). Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω) and describes how strongly a component opposes current.

sections.heading: Ohm's Law
sections.text: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across it. The relationship is V = IR.

content.example: A resistor has a resistance of 4 Ω and a potential difference of 12 V across it. The current is I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A.
content.summary: Current is measured in amperes, potential difference in volts and resistance in ohms. Ohm's Law relates these quantities for an ohmic conductor under constant physical conditions.

xh.title: Iisekethe Zombane noMthetho kaOhm
xh.intro: Iisekethe zombane zivumela intlawulo yombane ukuba ihambe kumacandelo aqhagamshelweyo. I-voltage, i-current kunye ne-resistance zichaza indlela isekethe esebenza ngayo.
xh.summary: I-current ilinganiswa ngee-amperes, i-voltage ngee-volts, ne-resistance ngee-ohms. UMthetho kaOhm udibanisa ezi zinto xa iimeko zifanelekile.

quiz.question: Which equation represents Ohm's Law?
quiz.explanation: Ohm's Law is expressed as V = IR, where V is potential difference, I is current and R is resistance.

quiz.question: A 6 Ω resistor is connected across a 12 V supply. What current flows through it?
quiz.explanation: Using I = V/R, the current is 12/6 = 2 A.

quiz.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?
quiz.explanation: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A).
